rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the elution window and critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. A midrange temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Keep the solvent window and temperature fixed to test whether a shallower gradient resolves the central cluster. The last peak at 7.16 minutes leaves some room to improve resolution without incurring a time penalty.

The shallower gradient improved the critical pair from R 0.46 to 1.20. Raising temperature alone now tests whether a selectivity shift can finish resolving that pair while keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

The central peak spacings suggest that two compounds crossed elution order between 40 and 50 C. A further 5 C increase may separate them beyond the crossing while preserving adequate spacing elsewhere and keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

After the apparent elution-order crossing, a slightly steeper gradient may increase separation of the remaining critical pair. Shortening to 12 minutes tests that possibility while reducing the last-peak time.

Injection 5 reached the maximum CRF and remains the benchmark. Shorten the gradient by one grid step to test whether full resolution can be maintained with a faster separation, particularly for the two marginal central pairs.

Return to the successful 12-minute gradient and raise the starting organic fraction one step to bring elution earlier. This narrows the gradient window rather than shortening its duration, testing whether the marginal central pairs retain full resolution.

With the maximum-CRF method already secured, test a faster, higher-temperature regime for an alternative selectivity pattern. The central pair may cross elution order, so this run will establish whether further compression can recover full resolution.

Test whether raising the starting organic fraction separates the central pair further on the far side of its apparent elution-order crossing. This could deliver a faster fully resolved method, while the early pair still has some resolution margin.

The faster high-temperature methods trade one central overlap for another. Test the opposite temperature limit to seek a different, fully resolved elution pattern with the 10-minute gradient, retaining injection 5 as the maximum-score benchmark.

At 60 C, the critical pair appears to separate on the opposite side of its crossing, so a steeper gradient may improve it. Test a 6-minute gradient with the lower starting organic fraction to preserve spacing to neighboring peaks.

Return to the near-optimal conditions of injection 7 and lower the final organic fraction one grid step. The shallower gradient should improve its R 1.29 pair while retaining the other critical pair’s separation, potentially giving a second maximum-score method with better resolution margins.

Lower the final organic fraction one more step to bring the R 1.47 pair above full-resolution threshold. The other critical pair should remain near R 1.6, and the last peak should still elute comfortably before 10 minutes.

Trim the successful injection 5 gradient to end just above its estimated last-peak elution fraction of 0.57. Keeping the same gradient slope should preserve full resolution while removing the unused high-organic portion of the program.

With maximum CRF secured, test a narrower, shallower gradient for greater resolution margin around both critical pairs. Raising the starting organic fraction should partly offset the longer gradient, keeping the last peak below 10 minutes.

Lower the endpoint one grid step from injection 15 to improve its sole under-resolved pair. Its other critical pair has R 1.74, providing margin for a shallower gradient while the last peak should remain below 10 minutes.

Test a faster high-temperature alternative: a higher starting fraction may separate the crossed central pair, while a longer gradient should protect its neighboring pair. Monitor the first two peaks closely because their resolution may become limiting at this starting composition.

Revisit the promising 40 C selectivity with a shallower gradient to improve the previously limiting R 1.20 pair. Raising the starting fraction slightly should offset some added retention time, testing another route to full resolution near the 10-minute cutoff.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step from injection 18 to bring its last peak below 10 minutes. The slightly shallower slope may preserve full resolution, and the early pair has ample separation margin.

Test whether cooling strengthens separation of the limiting central pair enough to permit a shorter gradient than injection 19. The other central spacings will determine whether this lower-temperature selectivity can retain maximum CRF.

Refine between injections 12 and 13 with a gradient slope expected to bring both critical pairs above R 1.5. This trimmed, 10-minute program should retain maximum CRF with slightly earlier final elution than injection 13.

Test a slightly shallower gradient than injection 13 to increase separation of its R 1.67 pair while checking that the R 1.58 pair stays fully resolved. This explores resolution margin without expecting a time penalty, with maximum CRF already secured.

Refine injection 16 with a slightly shallower slope, targeting more balanced margins for its two critical pairs. The trimmed endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution fraction, and the last peak should stay below 10 minutes.

Test a gradient slope of 0.080 fraction/min, between the fully resolved 0.075 slope and the unsuccessful 0.090 slope. This probes whether the fastest maximum-score separation can be shortened further; injection 5 remains the benchmark if the central pair loses resolution.

Keep the successful gradient slope through the first nine peaks, then hold at 0.50 to test a shorter programmed gradient. The last peak may elute somewhat later during the hold, but should remain below 10 minutes; injection 5 already secures the maximum CRF.
